title: Discretionary budget money by district
question: When the Board of Supervisors adds money to the Mayor’s budget and tags it to a district, which districts get it, per resident?
finding: Of $750 million in add-backs read from FY2014-15 to FY2027-28, $109 million (14.5%) is tagged to a district. Individual items carry a district tag only in the lists for FY2014-15 to FY2018-19; from 2018 the Board instead set aside a roughly equal lump per district. Counting only the items that competed, District 2 received $99 per resident and District 6 $54; with the lumps the range is $167 to $111. Across the 11 districts the rank correlation between that figure and household income is -0.01: too few districts to read anything into it.
how: Board of Supervisors spending-plan lists (one final document per budget cycle), rows with a district in the district column; a row tagged to several districts is split equally; citywide roll-up lines that repeat the district section are left out. 72 district labels misread by text recognition (for example “Dll” for D11) were corrected by rule. In the five budget cycles from 2018 to 2022 the Board set aside a lump for each district (about $0.5 to $1 million each, itemized in a separate district section); the “open” columns leave those lumps out and count only items that competed in the main list. Per-resident figures use Census 2020-24 population.
limits: An add-back is a budget act. With only 11 districts no statistical link to resident characteristics can be claimed; the table shows the order and the profile side by side. Much add-back money is citywide and is not in this table; a district tag says where a program is aimed, not who benefits. Scanned lists were read by text recognition and some rows are garbled. Whether the money follows a supervisor’s seat on the budget committee or length of service cannot be seen in these lists. The hearing minutes, roll-call votes and appeal decisions now being collected would show who voted, who objected and what reason was recorded in each case.
